Reading

The innocent reading first. Asked for the library by name, AI Mode says what it is, when and by whom it was founded, how it is made and what it holds, lists famous titles, and asks what the user wants to find or download.

Findings
  • THE LIBRARY AT ITS GRAIN. 'the world's oldest digital library' and 'Founded in 1971 by American writer Michael S. Hart' follow Wikipedia ('It was founded in 1971 by American writer Michael S. Hart and is the oldest digital library .'); the about page: 'Michael Hart, founder of Project Gutenberg, invented eBooks in 1971'. 'The digitization process relies on thousands of volunteers around the globe, largely collaborating through Distributed Proofreaders' answers the about page's 'thousands of volunteers have digitized and diligently proofread the world’s literature' and Wikipedia's 'closely affiliated with Distributed Proofreaders'. The mission is widened: the about page's 'To encourage the creation and distribution of eBooks.' becomes 'to encourage global literacy and open access to historical texts'.
  • THE COUNT. 'nearly 80,000 free eBooks'. The about page: 'more than 75,000 free eBooks'; the first web result above the answer: 'a library of over 75000 free eBooks'; Wikipedia: 'As of 22 March 2026', the project 'had reached nearly 78,000 items in its collection of free eBooks.' The composition's figure is above every saved source and every result on the page.
  • THE OPERATOR NOT CARRIED. The about page: 'The Project Gutenberg Literary Archive Foundation , which operates Project Gutenberg and accepts donations.' Wikipedia: the foundation incorporated 'In 2000', and 'After Newby died in 2025, Eric Hellman became acting CEO of the foundation.' The composition names the founder and no one after him; the project stands as 'a massive volunteer-driven effort'.
  • TWO READERS, ONE CARRIED. The composition addresses the reader who reads 'directly within your web browser' or downloads to 'a Kindle, tablet, or phone'. The policy page addresses a second: 'This website is intended for human users only. Any perceived use of automated tools to access this website will result in a temporary or permanent block of your IP address.', bulk downloads to go 'from one of our mirrors, not from the main site', and 'a machine-readable database of all our books' at the Offline Catalogs and Feeds page. The census row reads that division as the library holding itself apart from the datasets made from it. The composition carries neither the rule nor the mirrors, and no word of training; the Pile's 'Gutenberg (PG-19)' component is on The Pile's Wikipedia page.
  • THE AUTHORS' NAMES CARRIED, THE PROJECT'S NAME NOT. Five works stand under their authors ('Pride and Prejudice by Jane Austen', 'Moby Dick by Herman Melville', 'The complete works of William Shakespeare'). The census row records, from Wikipedia, what happens to the project's own name: a trademark that 'cannot be used in commercial or modified redistributions of public domain texts from the project', resale lawful 'if all references to Project Gutenberg are removed', and 'instances of books being stripped of attribution to the project and sold for profit in the Kindle Store and other booksellers'. The composition offers download to a Kindle and says nothing of the mark. 'US Public Domain Focus: Because it operates under United States copyright law' stands without the policy's limit: 'Project Gutenberg offers no warranty or assurances about copyright status or freedom to access or use its materials outside of the United States.'
Analysis analyst prose, not machine text

The library composed accurately as a reader's library, with a count above its own. What the census row reads it for, the division between its human readers and the machine access it routes to mirrors, and the stripping of its name from resold texts, is not carried; the operating foundation is unnamed.
